text.p: Secessionist leader Umberto Bossi proclaimed a self-styled "republic" in Italy's affluent north on Sunday, undeterred by scant support for his separatist push and a huge pro-unity rally in Milan.

To the backdrop of the Venice lagoon and solemn music, the firebrand leader of the Northern League declared a "federal republic of Padania" at a rally closing a three-day "March to the Sea" from the Alpine source of the River Po.

"We, the peoples of Padania, do solemnly proclaim: Padania is a federal, independent and sovereign republic," read the declaration, recited by Bossi after he arrived in Venice by catamaran at the head of a flotilla of small craft.
"And for support of this declaration we mutually pledge to each other our lives, our fortunes and our sacred honour," it read, echoing the 1776 American declaration of independence.

Aides to Bossi lowered the Italian flag and raised a white and green standard bearing the leaf symbol of the League's unrecognised, would-be "republic" before other speakers read out a "bill of rights" and a "transitional constitution".
The ceremony took place before a crowd estimated by police at fewer than 20,000 people, many wearing the League's trademark green shirts, and by the movement at up to 70,000.
It capped a quasi-religious weekend trek down the Po by Bossi which failed to draw anywhere near the more than one million followers he had hoped would throng his route.

His secessionist quest was instead upstaged by pro-unity rallies across Italy, including one in Milan where police estimated at least 150,000 people had joined a march organised by the hard-right National Alliance party.

Virtually all the rallies were peaceful but in Chioggia, at the south end of the Venice lagoon, witnesses said three people were slightly hurt in scuffles between police and pro-unity marchers led by neo-fascist southern politician Giancarlo Cito.

In Milan, the north's biggest city and headquarters of Bossi's League, National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini told a sea of people waving Italian flags that secession was an "insult to history and an insult to reason".
"Italy is here. It won't be insulted and it won't be divided," Fini said.
He called for court action after Bossi declared on Saturday that one of the first acts of a "provisional government of Padania" would be to recruit volunteers to a separatist militia.
The implicit threat of a violent path to independence, which Bossi has said he hopes will come within a year, also drew a sharp rebuke from President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro.
Scalfaro, a northerner himself, told a trade fair in southern Italy that while the state would guarantee free speech it would not tolerate incitement to "illegal acts".
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government has faced political flak for paying scant attention to Bossi's threat, responded by renewing a pledge to work for federal reform.
"Unity and autonomy must travel together in our country," Prodi said. "I'm not interested in Bossi...Federalism is born from concrete facts".

Bossi's League, founded in 1984, has thrived on frustration in the north with high taxes and stifling central government bureaucracy and public disaffection with mainstream parties in the wake of devastating political corruption scandals.

It won an unexpected 10.6 percent of votes at a general election in April but failed to gain the balance of power in parliament, a defeat Bossi's critics say explains his switch to a secessionist from a federalist agenda.

The absence of large crowds at Bossi's weekend rallies appeared to confirm the results of recent local elections in the north which punished the League and opinion polls which have shown overwhelming opposition to secession.
Bossi, who has dismissed reports of the low turnout as Italian "media lies", told the Venice rally he would now look to the United Nations and the European Union for recognition.
Diplomats say any official acknowledgement of "Padania", a concept with no ethnic or linguistic basis and which Bossi says could stretch as far south as Umbria in central Italy, is highly unlikely.
